routeb.note: Trace: one node's share (1/24, sessions kept together) of 2026-09-18 11:05–11:15 UTC, 727 requests, engines started cold. The DSpark engine's 106 s TTFT is queueing: its max running requests is 128 (the CUDA-graph envelope) and cold prefills of 50–650k prompts in 8k chunks stall decode across the DP lockstep, so slots are held for minutes and arrivals wait. Production sees 98.9% cache hits because sessions continue; a cold replay does not. The staircase warms the caches with the preceding 30 minutes first, which is the fair measurement.

summary: Where we are, in one breath: the vendor's demo as shipped did 0.72 M TPM per GPU. Two fixes (a Triton recompile patch and 8 tokenizer workers) and one swap (the older engine build that keeps DSpark on CUDA graphs) took the same node to 3.20 M per GPU on the manual's static frame, 46% of the 7 M north star. On real production traffic with warm caches the same node sustains about 1 M per GPU (2× one node's share) before TTFT runs away, because tp8/dp8 DP attention makes every prefill chunk stall decode on all eight ranks. The production-shaped 4×tp2 layout under a KV router is running now to attack exactly that.

glossary: MiniMax's 09-27 demo doc §3.2 launched exactly as written: their 09-27 engine (commit 024129fb), tp8/ep8/dp8, DSpark block 7, HiCache 192 GB, training-matched numerics. On that build the numerics flag forces DSpark to run without CUDA graphs ("eager"), so decode is 13–42 tok/s per stream.
The same launch with our Triton recompile fix. Same eager decode, so same ceiling.
The 09-27 engine with DSpark switched off (normal decode, which keeps its CUDA graphs) and HiCache on. Today's highest static-frame number once the frontend was fixed, but slow per stream.
The frontend fix: the engine's single HTTP/tokenizer process encoded each 80k prompt twice and admitted ~2 requests/s. Eight worker processes lift that.
The winning setup above: MiniMax's earlier 09-22 engine plus our DSpark port, which keeps CUDA graphs and therefore real spec-decode speed.

The M3 supplier manual's TPM test: one 80k-token prefix cached, 128 new tokens, 600 output tokens, random-token text. Because the text is random, spec decode accepts almost nothing there; it understates DSpark.

Replay of the production access log (real prompts, sessions, images, streaming flags) with the real arrival times. 1× = one node's share of production traffic at real speed; 2× = the same requests sent twice as fast (double the load); 4× = four times.

Route B held at 1×, 2×, 4×, 6×, 8× of a node's share for 5 minutes each after warming the caches with the preceding 30 minutes; the level where TTFT or errors break is the node's real-traffic capacity.
chart_note: Concurrency in parentheses is where the configuration peaked or was measured. The DSpark-graphs row is at c128 with 2.8 s TTFT (its max running requests is 128, the graph envelope); plain's 2.92 M is at c512, saturated with 29 s TTFT, and 2.11 M at the same c128.
pareto_note: Gains are measured at c128 on the static frame (plain 1 worker 0.91 → 8 workers 2.11 → DSpark graphs 3.20). Pending bars are drawn at an equal share of the remaining 3.80 M; their real sizes are unknown. The kernel patch removed 5-second stalls but adds no TPM on this frame; HiCache is not exercised by a single shared prefix.

staircase.title: Longitudinal capacity on real traffic: winning setup (tp8/dp8 DSpark graphs, 8 workers), caches warmed, 90.9% hit
columns: load level (× one node's share of today's fleet peak)
rows: not reached (trace exhausted behind the backlog)
staircase.note: Node's session-bucketed share (1/24) of the 09-27 15:00–16:00 UTC peak hour, 2,939 requests, 2,938 succeeded (1 read timeout), replayed after a warm-up with the preceding 30 minutes. Real-traffic capacity of this setup ≈ 2–2.5× one node's share ≈ 2 req/s ≈ 1 M TPM per GPU at p99 TTFT under 20 s. Production p50 TTFT on the same requests was 0.23 s, per-stream 210 tok/s (ours 25 at p50 across the run).
